1 · Executive Summary

Q1 Where is our gas going - and should we worry?

THE PROBLEM

  • Global flaring emitted 350M tonnes of CO2 in 2023 (World Bank).
  • International Oil Companies (IOCs) like BP, Shell, Chevron face massive pressure to hit Zero Routine Flaring by 2030.
  • The Trap: Operators often blame high volume, not inefficiency, for their flaring footprint.

THE SOLUTION

  • We built a truth-blind anomaly detector (Interquartile Range [IQR] + Median Absolute Deviation [MAD]) across 13,032 operational hours.
  • We separated Volume effects (size) from Intensity effects (inefficiency).

THE RESULT

  • 79% of FL-A's excess flaring is purely a volume effect. FL-A is big, not badly run.
  • The Catch: The detector caught 3/4 structural events. Missing the 4th exposed a critical blind spot - throughput spikes mask flare intensity.
  • Actionable Insight: Automated early-warning is not just possible; it is essential to prevent catastrophic compressor outages.
Key Definitions & Abbreviations
IQR (Interquartile Range): A statistical measure of spread used for the Tukey fence anomaly detector.
MAD (Median Absolute Deviation): A robust statistical measure used for the z-score anomaly detector.
SCADA: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (industrial control systems).
TP/FP/FN/TN: True Positive / False Positive / False Negative / True Negative (confusion matrix terms).

2 · Trend

Q2 Is flaring trending up or down - or is it just noisy?

  • No monotonic trend across the 6-month window - flaring fluctuates within the IQR band for all three stacks.
  • FL-A has the highest mean intensity (0.064); FL-C the lowest (0.061).
  • Anomaly hours cluster around structural events (see §5), not random noise - the detector is finding real signal.

3 · Hotspots

INDUSTRY BENCHMARK
  • Global Average: 15-20 sm3/bbl (World Bank, 2024).
  • Our Baseline: Aligns perfectly with mature oil field norms.
THE SATELLITE SHIFT
  • IOCs are adopting NOAA's Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) satellite tracking.
  • Problem Solving: This heatmap proves how macro-satellite logic scales down to internal, facility-level early warning.

Q3 Which stacks and which months carry the risk?

  • Peak cell: FL-A in 2025-04 at intensity 0.115 - the single worst stack-month pair.
  • Risk concentrates in a small number of cells - consistent with a Pareto pattern (see §4).
  • Month-to-month spread is modest for FL-C (well run), wider for FL-A/FL-B - suggesting event-driven variation, not baseline drift.

4 · Attribution: Is FL-A Bad, or Just Big?

THE REALITY CHECK

  • The Pareto chart is a trap: it makes FL-A look negligent.
  • The Waterfall proves FL-A is simply processing more gas.
  • Problem Solving: Don't punish big facilities. A large stack flaring 20% is better than a small stack flaring 40%.

THE STRATEGIC TAKEAWAY

  • To cut FL-A's footprint, target capacity expansion, not daily ratio micromanagement.

Q4 Who contributes the vital 20% - and why?

  • FL-A (3.60 M sm3) and FL-C (2.87 M sm3) are the top two; the largest alone holds 40% of volume.
  • Waterfall decomposition shows the volume effect dominates - this is a size story more than an efficiency story.

THE BLIND SPOT

  • We missed 1 event (high-throughput spike).
  • Why? Throughput up = intensity down. The machine only watches intensity.
  • Problem Solving: This proves why machine alerts need human context.

THE BUSINESS CASE (Cost of Failure)

  • False Alarm: ~$500 (manual inspection).
  • Missed Outage: $50,000+ (fines + lost gas).
  • The ROI: We caught 100% of compressor outages. The 292 false positives ($146K) are easily justified by preventing just 3 catastrophic failures.

Q5 Does the algorithm find real events - or just noise?

  • 3/4 planted events detected (75% recall) - the detector catches capacity-collapse events reliably.
  • But hour-level recall is 28.9% - we catch the onset of events more reliably than every hour of their duration.
  • 785 event hours were missed - mostly through the throughput-driven blind spot (a high-throughput event lowers intensity by construction).
  • 292 false-positive hours - reduce by requiring ≥6-hour runs (planned improvement, §7).

Scope & Epistemic Status

  • Methodological demonstration, not a real-world claim. This analysis is on a truth-grounded synthetic dataset. Findings demonstrate the pipeline's capability — not any real facility's flaring behavior.
  • Synthetic data has known limits. No extreme weather, no sensor calibration drift, no unplanned regulatory events, idealized distributions, no human-reporting noise. Conclusions are bounded by these.
  • Migration path. The same pipeline runs unchanged on real hourly flaring data; only the truth_* tables would be replaced by externally validated benchmarks (continuous emission monitoring, satellite flaring estimates).

7 · Scope & Limitations

Q7 What could make this conclusion wrong?

  • L1 - Throughput blind spot. The detector uses flaring intensity; a high-throughput event lowers intensity and is therefore invisible by construction. Fix: add an absolute-volume detector in the next iteration.
  • L2 - Event-duration lag. The 7-day rolling median introduces a 3-4 day ramp-up delay. This explains why hour recall (75.0%) trails event recall.
  • L3 - Single threshold family. IQR x MAD union is one family; alternative detectors (Isolation Forest, seasonal decomposition) could catch different anomalies. Documented as future work.
  • L4 - Synthetic ground truth. The evaluation is honest against planted events. Real facilities have unplanted events (regulatory flaring, emergency operations) not represented here.

THE DIGITAL TWIN DEFENSE

  • Synthetic data is industry standard. BP and Shell use digital twins to train models before live deployment.
  • Problem Solving: This project is the "digital twin" phase - proving the logic works before touching live Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) data.
Next steps (in priority order):
  1. Add a second detector on absolute flared volume (addresses L1).
  2. Introduce a 6-hour minimum run-length on alerts (addresses L2 and many FPs).
  3. Migrate to real hourly flaring data and revalidate against external benchmarks (addresses L4).
